rendered:
Answer: the LLTO-2 coating retained the most capacity after cycling at 0.5C[1] for 200 cycles[2]. The paper reports: LLTO coated NCM retained about 85.5%, 57.2% and[3] 86.2% for LLTO-0.5, LLTO-1 and LLTO-2 respectively[4]. So LLTO-2 was highest, LLTO-0.5 was close behind, and LLTO-1 was lowest. Compared with pristine NCM, the uncoated material only retained 56.6% of its initial discharge capacity after 200 cycles[5], so the LLTO coating gave a large gain in capacity retention over the pristine material.

Why the 2 mol.% coating[6] lowered rate capability: the paper says the LLTO coating generally improved rate capability, This increase in rate capability is attributed to high[7] ionic conductivity of the LLTO coating layer[8]. However, with that coating the rate capability decreased, and the authors suggest this may be due to the increase in the[9] thickness of the coating layer, resulting in the suppression of electron transfer process during charge/discharge cycling[10]. This is a hedged explanation offered by the authors; the document does not measure the electron transfer directly, and it does not explain why LLTO-1 retained so little capacity.
